idiom_name: hand-written name-keyed registry (HashMap plus trait objects); libloading for dynamic libraries
implementation_notes: Rust has no ambient name resolution, so the lookup service is a value the program builds: a HashMap from &str or String keys to trait objects, constructors or function pointers, populated by explicit registration, with the map's ownership and the trait-object indirection replacing the classic service handle. Missing names are representable in the type system instead of being a stringly runtime convention - get returns Option, and entry()/or_insert controls what happens on a duplicate binding. For genuinely dynamic resources, libloading wraps the platform loader safely: Library::new(name) loads a shared library and Library::get::<Symbol<fn()>>(b"symbol") resolves a symbol whose lifetime is tied to the Library, so a resolved function cannot outlive its library; nothing is cached behind your back, so re-resolution means building a new registry or loading a newer library.
pitfalls: A name-keyed HashMap silently replaces an existing binding on insert; use entry().or_insert()/try_insert or return an error when the name is already bound.
A global registry needs interior mutability plus Send + Sync (Mutex, RwLock, LazyLock); a HashMap of Box<dyn Trait> is not Sync, and hiding it in a static without synchronisation is a data race.
libloading::Symbol borrows the Library, so returning the symbol outlives the load and fails to compile; move owned data out, or keep symbol and library inside one struct so the borrow stays explicit.
